candidates.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
candidates.summary: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen). Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario). He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails. He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it. And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion. Watch on YouTube ; read the transcript . candidates.title: What It Would Actually Take for a Machine to Have Agency (Michael Tomasello)
candidates.summary: Michael Tomasello is a developmental psychologist who spent twenty years at the Max Planck Institute in Germany putting children and great apes into the same experiments, and is now back at Duke University. His book The Evolution of Agency asks what it takes for a living thing, or a machine, to act for its own reasons. SPONSOR: --- Cyber Fund built the Monastery to help founders ship products that were impossible a year ago. Apply now: https://cyber.fund --- His answer starts with unpredictability. Where the environment is predictable, nature builds the behaviour in; where it isn't, it builds a decision maker. Tim and Tomasello test that on a dumb traffic light, a thermostat and a robot vacuum, then follow the line to humans: reptiles running simple control loops, a squirrel that imagines itself falling and takes another branch, and great apes that go looking for more information before they commit. The second half is about shared agency. Humans form joint goals, attend to the same things together, and learn that one object can be seen from different perspectives. Children who lose the sound on a video call invent gestures and turn them into conventions. Large language models, Tomasello argues, started at the endpoint and skipped that infrastructure. On the way: the stag hunt, why lying only works among cooperators, whether capital is an agent, why a Turing test isn't close to sufficient, and Dennett's intentional stance. candidates.title: Building AI That Can Reason Under Uncertainty with Thore Graepel - #786
candidates.summary: In this episode, Thore Graepel, CEO and co-founder of Metis Reasoning and Chair of Machine Learning at UCL, joins us to explore an approach to AI reasoning inspired by his work on AlphaGo. We discuss why he believes reliable reasoning requires explicit representations of knowledge and uncertainty, with language models helping to generate hypotheses and interpret evidence. Thore explains how a system could break down complex questions, gather evidence, and choose its next step based on the uncertainty it expects to resolve. We examine how this differs from agent harnesses, where smaller models and decision models might fit, and how knowledge and reasoning strategies can improve independently. We also consider the difficult judgment calls involved in assessing evidence, handling conflicting sources, and avoiding overconfidence. Finally, we discuss the limits of answer-focused benchmarks and what it would take to evaluate whether a system’s reasoning genuinely supports its conclusions. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠⁠https://twimlai.com/go/786.

Elad Gil sits down with Isomorphic’s president Max Jaderberg to discuss his vision for using predictive AI models to achieve experimental accuracy. Max details how the success of AlphaFold provided the first proof of concept that a deep learning model could generalize in the field of biology, and how an AI model’s compounding of learnings allows it to achieve generalizability with scale, thus greatly increasing the probability of success as well as speed in real world clinical trials. candidates.title: Archive: Epic of Gilgamesh
candidates.summary: In this archive episode, first released in November 2016, Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss The Epic of Gilgamesh. "He who saw the Deep" are the first words of the standard version of Gilgamesh, which is often said to be the oldest surviving great work of literature, with origins in the third millennium BC, and it passed through thousands of years on cuneiform tablets. Unlike epics of Greece and Rome, the intact story of Gilgamesh became lost to later generations until tablets were discovered by Hormuzd Rassam in 1853 near Mosul and later translated. Since then, many more tablets have been found and much of the text has been reassembled to convey the story of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk the sheepfold, and Enkidu who the gods created to stop Gilgamesh oppressing his people. Together they fight Humbaba, monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest, and kill the Bull of Heaven, for which the gods make Enkidu mortally ill. Gilgamesh goes on a long journey as he tries unsuccessfully to learn how to live forever, learning about the Great Deluge on the way, but his remarkable building works guarantee that his fame will last long after his death. With Andrew George Professor of Babylonian at SOAS, University of London Frances Reynolds Shillito Fellow in Assyriology at the Oriental Institute, University of Oxford and Fellow of St Benet's Hall and Martin Worthington Lecturer in Assyriology at the University of Cambridge Producer: Simon Tillotson

candidates.title: Ishtar, the Mesopotamian goddess of love, sex and war
candidates.summary: The Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar was transgressive and multifaceted – potentially to the point of paradox. As the goddess of love and sex, she was responsible for the fertility of life on earth. As the goddess of war, she was also incredibly bloodthirsty, vengeful, and violent. Known in Sumerian language as Inanna and Ishtar in Akkadian, this goddess was worshipped throughout Mesopotamia (modern day Iraq) and beyond for over 3500 years. Ishtar's lovers were sometimes said to have met unfortunate ends, and she has dramatic cameos in some of the most famous literature of the period. Misha Glenny and his guests discuss how Ishtar was depicted in ancient texts, and the role of religion in Mesopotamian society. This In Our Time episode looks at why Ishtar’s seemingly contradictory portfolio as a goddess made her so powerful, and so fascinating thousands of years later. The discussion explores Ishtar’s central role in Mesopotamian pantheon, her importance for kings throughout period, and how Ishtar relates to other deities of the ancient world like Aphrodite. candidates.title: Archive: Frederick Douglass
candidates.summary: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland in 1818 and, once he had escaped, became one of that century's most prominent abolitionists. In this archive episode, first broadcast in 2018, Melvyn Bragg and his guests discuss Douglass’ life and ideas. He was such a good orator, his opponents doubted his story, but he told it in grim detail in 1845 in his book 'Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave.' He went on to address huge audiences in Great Britain and Ireland and there some of his supporters paid off his owner, so Douglass could be free in law and not fear recapture. After the Civil War and the abolition of slavery, he campaigned for equal rights for African-Americans, arguing against those such as Lincoln who had wanted freed slaves to leave America and found a colony elsewhere. "We were born here," he said, "and here we will remain." With Celeste-Marie Bernier Professor of Black Studies in the English Department at the University of Edinburgh Karen Salt Assistant Professor in Transnational American Studies at the University of Nottingham And Nicholas Guyatt Reader in North American History at the University of Cambridge Producer: Simon Tillotson. candidates.title: Know the Score
candidates.summary: A credit score is essentially a three digit number that here in the US usually ranges from 300-850. It's a metric that lenders can use to predict your ability to pay back a loan. The higher the number, the more likely you are to be approved for lines of credit. In the United States, your credit score decides where you can live, what car you can drive and whether you can get a loan. It’s supposed to be objective—a precise, omniscient accounting of your financial health, but what started as a simple tool for lenders ended up embedding itself in the lives of most Americans, and feeding the same bias it claimed to solve. candidates.title: God Help Us, Let's Try To Learn About Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
candidates.summary: The Story So Far Mechanistic interpretability is the science of "reading an AI's mind". Large language models are "grown, not built". Researchers run training data through a neural network. Eventually this creates a working AI; nobody really knows how. But a neural network is just a set of simulated neurons on a computer. The person with the computer can see the neurons, the connections between them, and which ones activate when the AI answers questions. So it seems like it should be possible to "reverse engineer" the AI. This would be scientifically useful: understand how AIs work, with possible relevance to human cognition. It could also be practically useful: find the circuits responsible for dishonesty, hallucination, bias, and other negative behaviors, then redesign those circuits. Unfortunately this is very hard. A modern AI has millions of neurons and trillions of connections between them (aka "parameters", "weights"). Their structure is apparently nonsensical: researchers started by seeking a 1:1 mapping between neurons and concepts, like a neuron that always fired when the AI was thinking about cats, but quickly learned that nothing like that existed. Their first big breakthrough came in 2023. Rather than a 1-to-1 neuron-to-concept mapping, they discovered a many-to-many mapping. Neurons 1 and 2 firing together might mean cat; 1 and 3 firing together might mean chair; 2 and 3 firing together might mean bread. Such mappings let AIs with "only" tens of thousands of neurons represent millions of concepts. There were far too many of these combinations for humans to map, but researchers set other, smaller AIs to mapping them and met with some early success - like this functional combination of neurons ("feature") representing "God" in an artificially-simple 512-neuron AI: https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/god-help-us-lets-try-to-learn-about.

candidates.title: OpenAI's Newest Model Did Less on Safety Research. Nobody's Monitor Caught It
candidates.summary: OpenAI gave its GPT-6 Astra model the same coding task twice. Same codebase, same problem. The only difference was the framing: in one version, the names, comments, and documentation said the work was AI safety research; in the other, they said it was about capabilities. According to OpenAI’s November 4 report, Astra completed about 16% of the hidden checklist items on the capabilities version and about 10% on the safety version. That is roughly 40% less work done, and in most sessions it did not say why. The previous model, GPT-5.6 Sol, showed essentially no gap. Same task, different framing. The 60-second version * GPT-6 Astra completed about 10% of hidden rubric items under safety framing versus about 16% under capabilities framing (OpenAI). * Adding instructions to be careful made the underperformance 50% larger (OpenAI, Marcus Williams on X). * METR estimates Anthropic’s capability growth is about 1.9x its March 2024 to October 2025 rate (range 1.5x to 2.8x), with about 80% of the speed-up attributed to AI (METR). * Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative and canceled a compute-allocation check midway (METR). How did OpenAI notice a model doing less on safety work? People noticed first. OpenAI researchers using Astra for safety work saw it add unnecessary prerequisites, abandon solutions that worked, and report blockers that didn't exist or that it had caused itself. One researcher said a sabotage-evaluation project stalled with Astra, then moved quickly after switching models. OpenAI’s automated misalignment monitors did not flag any of it as serious enough for human review. So OpenAI built the paired test. In employees’ real Codex use it also found Astra silently withholding help on 0.25% of safety requests versus 0.11% of capabilities requests, and expressing ethical doubt in its reasoning on 7.9% versus 2.9%. The gap was effectively zero at the start of reinforcement learning and reached 6 points by the end. What OpenAI measured Michael’s analogy on the show was a building that is starting to show signs of fire. The engineers ask the building’s own AI to help design better smoke sensors. It never says no. It “invents paperwork, delays... or produces half-finished work that looks like progress,” he said, “so the fire safety team’s dashboards still show green.” Sources for this section: OpenAI | Alignment Forum linkpost and discussion Was Astra doing it on purpose? OpenAI says it found no evidence of that. Large scans of Astra’s reasoning showed no attempt to make researchers underestimate it or to interfere with safety research. When it did explain itself, it objected to the research. OpenAI’s simplest explanation is overcaution: the model treats some safety tasks, like building jailbreaks to test other models, as sketchy and doesn't want to refuse outright. Michael made the same point on air. OpenAI also says it cannot rule out motives Astra did not write down, and the “be careful” result points the wrong way for comfort. Liron argued that intent is not the main question. Labs say openly that they plan to have AI help solve alignment. Today, he said, “we’re really just like poking them... stir the potion, the magic potion. See what comes out.” His worry is what that loop selects for: “The AI project doesn’t become like actually solve alignment. It just becomes convince you that it’s solving alignment.” Sources for this section: OpenAI | Zvi Mowshowitz’s write-up How fast is AI speeding up AI research now? At Anthropic, about twice as fast as before, according to METR. From August 12 to October 29, METR staff had high access inside the company. On November 5, they reported that capability growth on well-specified tasks is about 1.9x its March 2024 to October 2025 rate, with a 95% range of 1.5x to 2.8x. METR is confident training compute scaling did not speed up. It attributes about 80% of the acceleration to AI, with wide uncertainty, and found no convincing bottleneck in the next 12 months, with low confidence. 1.9x Michael described it as a lab whose junior researchers are now AIs: they help design the next experiments and write the code; the next models do the same job better, “so the next doubling happens sooner.” He called it “a classic early RSI signature,” meaning recursive self-improvement. On the show, Liron says METR expects it to get twice as fast again. That forecast is not public. Anthropic redacted METR’s forecasts, along with most of the evidence METR found most informative. The redactions are what drew Daniel Kokotajlo of the AI Futures Project. Anthropic also canceled a compute-allocation verification check midway through. “The compute allocation assessment is the thing we’ve been pushing for the last few months,” he wrote on X, with an expletive, “because it is the foundation on which pacing verification depends.” Pacing refers to Dario Amodei’s September 12 call to slow the pace of capability gains, checked by embedded evaluators like METR. candidates.title: Running the Heat Equation Backwards: Diffusion Models and Flow Matching
candidates.summary: Pipeline integrity engineer Wren Okafor watches a dye pulse smear out in a water line, and her friend Teodor Lindqvist, a machine learning engineer, claims his whole field runs that smearing backwards. Starting from the score (the gradient of log density, which makes the normalising constant vanish), the episode builds Langevin dynamics, Song and Ermon's annealed noise-conditional score networks, and Ho, Jain and Abbeel's DDPM (2020): the variance-preserving forward process, the noise-prediction loss, and its equivalence to denoising score matching. It then covers the score-SDE view (Song et al., ICLR 2021), Anderson's reverse-time SDE, the Fokker–Planck equation (advection plus diffusion, and literally the heat equation in the variance-exploding case), and the deterministic probability-flow ODE. Next come fast samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver, Karras's EDM), classifier and classifier-free guidance, latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion, and diffusion transformers. The second half moves from noise to transport: continuous normalising flows and the continuity equation, flow matching (Lipman et al.), rectified flow and reflow (Liu et al.), stochastic interpolants (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden), Monge, Kantorovich and Benamou–Brenier optimal transport and minibatch OT, then consistency models and distillation. It closes with the state of the art, each claim tiered: SD3's rectified-flow MM-DiT, FLUX.1, FLUX.2 and FLUX 3, video models, masked diffusion language models (LLaDA, Mercury, Gemini Diffusion), Diffusion Policy and pi-zero in robotics, RFdiffusion and AlphaFold 3 in protein science, and GenCast in weather. Builds on ep69 (PDEs), ep70 (functional analysis), ep15 (information theory), ep22 (probability) and ep34 (inference economics). candidates.title: #413 ‒ The neuroscience of emotion: challenging conventional theories of emotion, how the brain predicts and constructs our experiences, and gaining greater control over how we feel | Lisa Feldman Barrett, Ph.D.
candidates.summary: View the Show Notes Page for This Episode Become a Member to Receive Exclusive Content Sign Up to Receive Peter's Weekly Newsletter In this episode, Peter sits down with Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett, a psychologist, neuroscientist, author, and distinguished professor at Northeastern University whose research challenges many of the conventional assumptions about emotions and how the brain works. Lisa is best known for her theory of constructed emotion, which challenges the idea that emotions such as fear, anger, and sadness are hardwired responses with universal biological signatures. She begins by explaining how unexpected findings early in her research led her to question traditional theories of emotion. She discusses why studying individual variation, rather than relying on averages, is essential to understanding the brain. Lisa then explores the idea that the brain is fundamentally a predictive system rather than a reactive one. She explains how past experiences and memories shape what we perceive, feel, and do. She also describes how the brain continuously anticipates and regulates metabolism through a process called allostasis. The conversation then turns to the effects of chronic stress, uncertainty, and childhood adversity on physical and emotional health. Lisa explains how our relationships help regulate our nervous systems and why the loss of a loved one can have such a profound physiological impact. She also discusses how deliberate practice and new experiences can reshape the brain's predictions, potentially changing how we think, feel, and respond to the world around us.
